title: The warm dusk search
scenario:
Your studio keeps about 2,000 assets for Marlow Outdoor, a tent brand. A search tool sits between the library and the model. The art director sends a brief and you decide how the search should work.

The catalogue lines and the search log in the exhibit are made up for this case.
exhibit:
Brief
  "A warm dusk photo of a tent, like A-231. Approved assets only, licensed
  through at least 2027."

Catalogue sample (made up)
  id     caption                                         approved  licence_until
  A-231  Warm lantern light on a canvas tent at dusk     yes       2028-06-30
  A-232  Orange tent on a hill at sunrise, clear sky      yes       2026-12-31
  A-233  Draft: tent at dusk, rough edit                  no        2028-06-30

Search log (made up)
  query: "cosy evening"
  result 1: A-231   (no word is shared with the query)

questions.prompt: Which search design fits the brief best?

options.text: Rank all 2,000 assets by closeness, then have the art director cross out any that are not approved.
options.explanation: Rules checked by hand are easy to miss. Approval and licence dates are exact facts and belong in a filter.

options.text: Search the captions for the words "approved" and "2027", and take the top three matches.
options.explanation: Captions describe what an image shows. Approval and licence dates are separate facts, so a word search would miss them.

options.text: Filter on approved and licence date first, then rank what is left by closeness to the warm dusk look.
options.explanation: Right. Both OpenAI (attributes and attribute filters) and Google (metadata filters) let you filter on facts. Rules go in filters, closeness goes in ranking.

options.text: Give the model all 2,000 images and ask which ones it likes best for a warm dusk tent photo.
options.explanation: This skips every rule and pays to read the whole library. The model should read only what search returns.

questions.prompt: The query "cosy evening" returns A-231 first, and no word is shared. Why?

options.text: Semantic search matches meaning. "Warm lantern light at dusk" is close to "cosy evening".
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI says semantic search surfaces relevant results even when they match few or no keywords.

options.text: The tool added a hidden "cosy" tag to A-231 when it was uploaded, and then matched on the tag.
options.explanation: Nothing in the docs says tags are added. The match comes from the meaning of the caption.

options.text: It is a bug. Search must always require at least one shared word before it can return a result.
options.explanation: That describes keyword search. Semantic search is built to find results with few or no shared words.

options.text: A-231 ranks first because it was the most recent file added to the library, and not for its meaning.
options.explanation: Recency is not part of how semantic search ranks. The ranking comes from how close the meanings are.

questions.prompt: The team uses OpenAI file search and wants to find assets by look. They plan to upload 1,500 JPG files. What is your advice?

options.text: Upload the JPG files. File search reads the pictures and ranks them by how they look to the model.
options.explanation: The supported-files table lists text and document formats, and no image types.

options.text: Rename the JPG files to .txt, so that the file search accepts them as text documents and indexes them.
options.explanation: A renamed picture is not text. The tool would index nothing useful from it.

options.text: Search only on file names, and keep each file name as short as possible for the search tool to use.
options.explanation: Short names carry little meaning. Captions hold the subject, look and mood that search needs.

options.text: Write a caption for each asset in a text file, with the asset id in each entry, and index that file.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's file search lists text and document formats, so the captions carry the meaning and the id leads back to the image.

questions.prompt: How do you check the search before the next campaign?

options.text: Run one query for "tent" and confirm that the first result has a tent in it, then call it done.
options.explanation: One easy query proves little. It will not show how the search handles real briefs.

options.text: Take ten past briefs, run them, and compare the top three results with what the art director chose.
options.explanation: Right. This is our habit: real briefs and a known good answer show where captions and filters need work.

options.text: Set the score threshold high. A high threshold proves that every result is allowed for use.
options.explanation: A score measures relevance to the query. It does not know about approval or licence.

options.text: Ask the model if the results look good. Its answer is the test, so no other check is needed.
options.explanation: A model can read what it is shown and miss what it was not shown. The art director's picks are the better test.
